excerpt: Paano magtanim ng almond? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant almendras (almond), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: A farm worker planting in a field

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant almendras. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

True almond is not grown in the Philippines: it needs a cold winter and a long dry summer, so only a rare hobby tree is kept in the cool highlands, such as around Baguio, and it seldom bears. The tree many Filipinos call almond or almendras is talisay, a different coastal tree that grows anywhere here. This short guide covers the few highland attempts with true almond.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant almendras
Trees are set out at the start of the rains, about May to July, in the highlands, on the driest, sunniest slope available. Rain at flowering spoils the nuts.
What you plant
Grafted trees of low chill almond types from a specialty nursery. Two types that flower together are needed, since most almonds need a partner to set nuts.
Paano magtanim ng almond, step by step
We count the first harvest at about 40 months (1,200 days). Most trees here never bear well. The crop is ready about 40 months after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before planting: Choose a dry, sunny slope
items.text: Pick the sunniest, driest high ground with deep soil that drains fast. Dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep with compost.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant two types together
items.text: Set two grafted trees of different types about 5 m apart at the same depth they grew, graft joint above the soil. Firm, water, stake and mulch.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Month 3: Prune to an open bowl
items.text: Keep three or four spreading branches, feed compost and a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every few months, and water only in long dry spells.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Month 40: Gather the nuts
items.text: We count the first crop at about 40 months. Pick nuts when the green hulls split open, and dry them in the sun before storing.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for almendras
Spacing
About 5 m between trees, at least two types close together.
Water
Mostly rain fed. Almond dislikes wet soil and rain at flowering.
Fertilizer
Compost and small amounts of complete fertilizer (14 14 14). To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows
Open bowl pruning, light feeding, keeping the ground dry and weed free.
When and how to harvest
Nuts are picked when the hulls split, dried in the sun, and shelled.
Common mistakes when planting almendras

items: Planting a single almond tree, which sets few or no nuts.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of almendras
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: For a nut tree that bears here, consider pili or cashew instead.
If you try almond, use low chill grafted types on dry highland slopes and keep notes.
Test the soil and feed by the result.
